cards.explanation: The answer is God. Paul, the apostle writing this letter, says, “Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children…” (Ephesians 5:1). The pattern isn't a hero down the street. It's the Father Himself, and beloved children get to copy Him.

The picture is Christ giving Himself up for us. Paul says to walk in love, “…just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God.” (Ephesians 5:2). The love he's pointing to is the love Christ already showed. Paul didn't have to go looking for an example.

The answer is False, because the text says the opposite. Paul writes, “…there must not be even a hint of sexual immorality, or of any kind of impurity, or of greed.” (Ephesians 5:3). Greed is on that list with no size limit. Not even a hint means not even a hint, friends, and I couldn't say it better.

The answer is True. Paul writes, “Nor should there be obscenity, foolish talk, or crude joking, which are out of character, but rather thanksgiving.” (Ephesians 5:4). Out of character means it doesn't fit who these believers are. And look at what he puts in its place, friends: thanksgiving.

The answer is False. Paul writes, “For of this you can be sure: No immoral, impure, or greedy person (that is, an idolater) has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” (Ephesians 5:5). He opens with “…you can be sure…” so there's nothing here to haggle over. I've tried haggling with my oven timer, and it never works either.

The note is the one that says an idolater. The verse reads “…(that is, an idolater)…” right after the words about the greedy person. Paul ties greed to idolatry in that one little aside. It's a short note, friends, but it packs a lot in.

The answer is the wrath of God. Paul says, “Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of such things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.” (Ephesians 5:6). He warns against being deceived with empty words, and then he names what is coming.

The answer is False, and the verse is short and clear: “Therefore do not be partakers with them.” (Ephesians 5:7). Paul never says to join them. He says not to be partakers with them, and he leaves it at that. Short verse, big point, friends.

The answer is as children of light. Paul says, “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light…” (Ephesians 5:8). Notice the order, friends: he tells them what they are before he tells them how to walk. The walk follows the light.

The answer is False, because it's not about pleasing other people. Paul says, “Test and prove what pleases the Lord.” (Ephesians 5:10). The Lord is the one whose pleasure the children of light are trying to learn. That's a much better aim than guessing what a crowd wants.

The word is expose. Paul says, “Have no fellowship with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them.” (Ephesians 5:11). Children of light don't join in, and they don't just look away either. The light does its work by showing things as they are.
The answer is True. Paul writes, “…everything that is illuminated becomes a light itself.” (Ephesians 5:13). The light doesn't just show things, friends. It says what it shines on becomes light too.

The promise is that Christ will shine on the sleeper. The saying goes, “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” (Ephesians 5:14). It tells the sleeper to wake up and rise, and it says Christ will shine on him. Paul introduces it with “So it is said:” so he's passing along a saying.
The answer is False. Paul writes, “…redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” (Ephesians 5:16). He calls the days evil, not good, and that's why the time matters, friends.

The word is Lord's. Paul says, “Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is.” (Ephesians 5:17). The opposite of foolish here is understanding the Lord's will. That's the thing to chase, friends.

The answer is the Spirit. Paul says, “Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit.” (Ephesians 5:18). Notice he doesn't just say stop, friends. He says what to take up instead.

The answer is False, because they aren't kept to yourself. Paul writes, “Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing and make music in your hearts to the Lord…” (Ephesians 5:19). It's both: to one another and in your hearts to the Lord. Nobody in that verse is asked to sing solo in a closet.

The word is always. Paul says, “…always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” (Ephesians 5:20). Not now and then, friends, but always, and for everything. That's a thankful way to live.
